ieltsReading.title: Learning in the garden
ieltsReading.text: When the primary school in a small town near the river opened its garden five years ago, many parents were doubtful. The head teacher, Ms Sophea, wanted children to learn science and maths by growing vegetables, but some families worried that it would take time away from reading and writing. Today, the garden covers about half of the school's land. Each class looks after its own section, and pupils measure how fast the plants grow, record the weather and calculate how much they can sell at the weekly market. The money pays for books and for school trips. According to the school's own records, pupils' maths results have improved every year since the garden began, although Ms Sophea admits that a new maths teacher, who joined at the same time, may also have made a difference. Not every school could copy the idea: the garden needs water all year, and in the dry season older pupils carry it from a well. Several schools in the province have visited, and two have started small gardens of their own.

statements.text: Some parents were not sure about the garden at first.
The garden is bigger than the school buildings.
statements.why: It covers half of the land; the buildings' size is never given.

statements.text: Every class grows the same vegetables.
statements.why: Each class has its own section, but the text does not say what they grow.

statements.text: Money from the market is spent on books.
statements.why: "The money pays for books and for school trips."

statements.text: Ms Sophea thinks the garden is the only reason maths results improved.
statements.why: She admits the new maths teacher may also have made a difference.

statements.text: In the dry season the garden's water comes from the river.
statements.why: Older pupils carry it from a well.

ieltsReading.title: Why we forget new words
ieltsReading.text: In the 1880s, the German researcher Hermann Ebbinghaus tested his own memory by learning lists of nonsense syllables and checking how many he could remember after different amounts of time. He found that most forgetting happens soon after learning: a lot is lost within the first day, and after that it is lost more slowly. He also found that reviewing material several times, with gaps between the reviews, made it last much longer than studying it many times in one sitting. Modern researchers call this the spacing effect, and many studies since then have confirmed it. Some language-learning apps now use it to decide when to show each word again. However, scientists point out that memory also depends on other things, such as sleep, interest in the subject and whether a word is used in real conversation. A word that you say to a friend may be remembered better than one you only read on a screen.

statements.text: Ebbinghaus tested his ideas on other people.
Forgetting is fastest soon after learning.
Other scientists of his time did not accept Ebbinghaus's work.
statements.why: The text says nothing about how scientists of his time reacted.

statements.text: Studying something many times in one session works better than spaced reviews.
statements.why: Spaced reviews made it last much longer.

statements.text: Sleep can affect how well we remember.
statements.why: Memory "also depends on other things, such as sleep".

statements.text: Most language-learning apps use the spacing effect.
statements.why: It says "some" apps use it; it does not say how many.

ieltsReading.title: The night market
ieltsReading.text: Every Friday and Saturday evening, the car park behind the town's main bus station becomes a night market. It started three years ago with about twenty food stalls, and it now has more than eighty, selling clothes, phone accessories and handmade jewellery as well as food. The market is run by a group of local sellers rather than by the town council, and each stall pays a small fee to cover cleaning and electricity. Most visitors are young people who come after work or college, but on Saturdays many families bring their children for the live music. The organisers say that the market has helped people who lost their jobs to start small businesses. Not everyone is happy, however. Some shop owners in the town centre complain that they have lost customers since the market opened, and people living nearby have asked for the music to end earlier. The organisers have agreed to stop the music at ten o'clock, but they say they have no plans to open on weekdays.

statements.text: The market takes place in a car park.
statements.why: "The car park behind the town's main bus station becomes a night market."

statements.text: The town council runs the market.
statements.why: It is run by local sellers "rather than by the town council".

statements.text: The stall fee has gone up since the market opened.
statements.why: The fee is mentioned, but not whether it has changed.
"On Saturdays many families bring their children."

statements.text: Some shop owners are unhappy about the market.
statements.why: They "complain that they have lost customers".

statements.text: The market will soon open on weekdays too.
statements.why: They "have no plans to open on weekdays".

ieltsListening.title: Booking a homestay
ieltsListening.intro: A woman phones a homestay to book a room. Complete the form.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Good morning, Green River Homestay. How can I help you?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Hello. I'd like to book a room for my husband and me, please.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Of course. Can I have your name?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: It's Sreymom. That's S, R, E, Y, M, O, M.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Thank you. And when would you like to come?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: We'd like to arrive on the fourteenth of April and stay for three nights.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That's fine. A double room is twenty-five dollars a night, with breakfast.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Great. Can you also book us a boat trip?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes. The boat trip leaves at seven thirty in the morning. Can I take a phone number?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Sure. It's oh one two, four five eight, nine oh three.

ieltsListening.title: Joining an English course
ieltsListening.intro: A man phones a language centre to join a class. Complete the form.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Good afternoon, City Language Centre.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Hi. I'd like to join the evening speaking class, please.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Certainly. What's your family name?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: It's Chhim. C, H, H, I, M.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: And your first name?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Dara. D, A, R, A.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Which level did you finish?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: I finished level six last term.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Then you'll be in level seven. The class is on Tuesdays and Thursdays, from six to half past seven.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: How much is it?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It's ninety dollars for ten weeks, and the book is twelve dollars.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And when does it start?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: On the third of March.

ieltsListening.title: A lost phone
ieltsListening.intro: A woman calls the lost property office at a bus station. Complete the form.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Bus station, lost property office. Can I help you?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Yes, I think I left my phone on a bus this morning.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Which bus was it?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: The number fifteen, to the airport.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: What time did you get off?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: At about ten past nine.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: And what does the phone look like?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: It's a black phone in a red case.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Can I have your name, please?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Vanna Kong. That's K, O, N, G.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: And a number where we can call you?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Please call my sister on oh nine seven, two two one, six oh four.
